**Summary of work done**

- Conducted targeted web searches for medical information relevant to postpartum week 3 (days 15‑21) covering:
  1. Breastfeeding challenges (milk supply, latch difficulties)
  2. Maternal mood changes (post‑partum depression/anxiety, baby blues)
  3. Infant growth spurts (typical timing, signs, management)
  4. Post‑partum checkup preparation (timing, what to expect, questions to ask)
- Retrieved high‑quality sources from reputable medical organizations (ACOG, NIMH, Mayo Clinic, Cleveland Clinic), peer‑reviewed literature (PMC), and trusted patient‑education sites.
- Compiled the sources into thematic lists with brief descriptions based on the search result snippets.

**Sources gathered**

*Breastfeeding challenges (supply & latch)*
1. **ACOG – Breastfeeding Challenges** (Committee Opinion, Feb 2021)  
   https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2021/02/breastfeeding-challenges  
   – Guidance on establishing milk supply, latch support, hand expression, and managing early difficulties.
2. **PMC – Breastfeeding difficulties in the first 6 weeks postpartum among mothers with chronic conditions**  
   https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9893695/  
   – Identifies “ineffective latch” cluster (high prevalence of sore nipples, latch problems, maternal fatigue).
3. **Physician Guide to Breastfeeding – Breastfeeding at 3‑6 Weeks Postpartum**  
   https://physicianguidetobreastfeeding.org/breastfeeding-basics/next-steps-3-6-weeks/  
   – Advises seeking professional help for positioning/latch if breastfeeding got off to a rocky start.
4. **UNICEF Europe & Central Asia – The 3‑month breastfeeding crisis**  
   https://www.unicef.org/eca/stories/3-month-breastfeeding-crisis-what-it-and-how-get-through-it  
   – Describes infant fussiness, refusal to latch, and on/off feeding patterns that can arise around this period.
5. **PMC – Breastfeeding Concerns at 3 and 7 Days Postpartum and Feeding Status at 2 Months**  
   https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3784292/  
   – Links early concerns about infant feeding difficulty and milk quantity to later breastfeeding cessation.

*Maternal mood changes*
6. **NIMH – Perinatal Depression**  
   https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/publications/perinatal-depression  
   – Notes that mood changes, anxiety, or unhappiness lasting >2 weeks may signal postpartum depression.
7. **Cleveland Clinic – Postpartum Depression (PPD): Causes, Symptoms & Treatment**  
   https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/9312-postpartum-depression  
   – Lists extreme sadness, severe mood swings, anxiety, loss of interest as possible PPD symptoms.
8. **PMC – Consequences of maternal postpartum depression: A systematic review**  
   https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6492376/  
   – Details maternal symptoms (appetite disturbance, guilt, irritability, suicidal thoughts) and infant outcomes.
9. **ACOG – Postpartum Depression FAQ**  
   https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/postpartum-depression  
   – Distinguishes baby blues (starts ~3 days postpartum) from clinical depression; provides resources.
10. **Mayo Clinic – Postpartum depression: Symptoms and causes**  
    https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/postpartum-depression/symptoms-causes/syc-20376617  
    – Overview of risk factors, symptoms, and treatment options.

*Infant growth spurts*
11. **Kids Central Pediatrics – Your 3‑Week Old**  
    https://kidscentralpediatrics.com/your-3-week-old/  
    – Expected weight regain plus a few ounces; importance of regular pediatric checkups.
12. **Pampers – All About Baby Growth Spurts: Signs, Timing, & Support**  
    https://www.pampers.com/en-us/baby/development/article/baby-growth-spurts  
    – Notes growth spurts commonly occur between 3‑6 weeks.
13. **Bay Area Breastfeeding & Education – The Infamous Growth Spurt: Five Tips for Survival**  
    https://www.bayareabreastfeeding.net/blog/2017/1/11/the-infamous-growth-spurt-five-tips-for-survival  
    – Typical timing: 6‑7 days, 2‑3 weeks, 6‑8 weeks; signs include increased hunger, fussiness.
14. **WhatToExpect – Baby Growth Spurts: When Infant Growth Spurts Happen and the Signs**  
    https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/ask-heidi/baby-growth-spurts.aspx  
    – Early‑month spurts around 1‑3 weeks and again at 6‑8 weeks.
15. **Summer Health – Understanding growth spurts in infants**  
    https://www.summerhealth.com/blog/6-month-growth-spurt  
    – For some babies, a spurt at 2‑3 weeks; signs: evening hunger, clinginess.

*Post‑partum checkup preparation*
16. **ACOG – What to Expect at a Postpartum Checkup—and Why the Visit Matters**  
    https://www.acog.org/womens-health/experts-and-stories/the-latest/what-to-expect-at-a-postpartum-checkup-and-why-the-visit-matters  
    – Recommends first checkup within 3 weeks; outlines typical components (physical exam, mood screening, contraception, feeding questions).
17. **March of Dimes – Your postpartum checkups**  
    https://www.marchofdimes.org/find-support/topics/postpartum/your-postpartum-checkups  
    – Advises a complete checkup no later than 12 weeks; emphasizes early visits to catch warning signs.
18. **Kaiser Permanente – Postpartum: First 6 Weeks After Childbirth**  
    https://healthy.kaiserpermanente.org/health-wellness/health-encyclopedia/he.postpartum-first-6-weeks-after-childbirth.abl1277  
    – Describes what’s covered: mood/PPD screening, pelvic exam, incision check (if C‑section), birth‑control discussion.
19. **WhatToExpect – Here's When You'll Have Your Postpartum Checkup and What You Can Expect**  
    https://www.whattoexpect.com/first-year/six-week-postpartum-checkup.aspx  
    – Notes the shift toward an initial visit within 3 weeks per ACOG guidance.
20. **Carnegie Imaging – Your First Postpartum Visit: What to Expect**  
    https://www.carnegieimaging.com/blog/your-first-postpartum-visit-what-to-expect/  
    – Typical timing (3‑12 weeks); list of common questions to ask the provider.

**Issues encountered**
- The `web_extract` tool failed because the current search backend (Brave Search free tier) does not support content extraction. Consequently, I could not retrieve full‑text articles directly; instead, I relied on the descriptive snippets returned by `web_search`. These snippets still provide sufficient information to identify credible, relevant sources for the requested topics.
- No local files were created or modified during this session. If a persistent record of these sources is desired, the list above can be saved to a file (e.g., `/home/azureuser/hermes-workspace/week3_medical_sources.md`) using standard shell commands outside of this toolset.

**What you received**
A curated set of 20 medical sources, organized by the four focus areas, each with a brief description of its relevance to week‑3 postpartum care. These can be used for further reading, patient education, or clinical reference.
